definition: The Constituent Likelihood Automatic Word-tagging System (CLAWS) is a program that performs part-of-speech tagging.
details: It was developed in the 1980s at Lancaster University by the University Centre for Computer Corpus Research on Language. It has an overall accuracy rate of 96–97% with the latest version (CLAWS4) tagging around 100 million words of the British National Corpus.

explainer.lead: CLAWS automatically adds part-of-speech labels to words, showing whether each word functions as a noun, verb, determiner, and so on. These labels make large text collections easier to search and study; CLAWS4 was used to tag around 100 million words of the British National Corpus.

tiers.eli5: Imagine putting a colored sticker on every word to show its job in a sentence: one color for naming words, another for action words, and so on. CLAWS does this automatically for lots of writing. That helps people study how language is used without labeling every word by hand.
tiers.practitioner: Use CLAWS when a corpus needs part-of-speech annotations for linguistic search or analysis. Treat the reported 96–97% overall accuracy as an aggregate result, not a guarantee for every text or ambiguous word, and inspect tags before relying on them in downstream work.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, CLAWS maps a token sequence w_1, ..., w_n to a corresponding part-of-speech tag sequence t_1, ..., t_n. It was developed in the 1980s at Lancaster University by the University Centre for Computer Corpus Research on Language. Its stated overall accuracy is 96–97%, so some tagging errors remain.

explainer.example: For the sentence “The cat sleeps,” an illustrative tagging labels “The” as a determiner, “cat” as a noun, and “sleeps” as a verb. Repeating this across a corpus makes patterns involving those word classes searchable.

usedIn.name: British National Corpus
usedIn.detail: CLAWS4 tagged around 100 million words of this corpus.

usedIn.name: Corpus linguistics
usedIn.detail: Part-of-speech tags support searches and studies of grammatical patterns in large text collections.

explainer.intuition: A word’s grammatical role becomes much more useful when it is recorded explicitly. CLAWS automates that labeling so entire corpora can be annotated rather than small samples.
howItWorks: Process the words in their sentences.
Assign a part-of-speech tag to each word.
Return the text with its grammatical labels.
explainer.whyItMatters: Automatic tagging turns plain text into grammatically annotated data at corpus scale. CLAWS4’s tagging of around 100 million words of the British National Corpus shows that scale.
misconceptions: Part-of-speech tagging labels word roles; it is not the same as producing a complete sentence parse.
An overall accuracy of 96–97% does not mean every individual word or text is tagged with that accuracy.

diagram.caption: CLAWS converts unlabeled text into part-of-speech-tagged text for corpus study.
